title: TikTok Misinformation and User Engagement in Female Pelvic Floor Conditions
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 74 high-engagement TikTok videos on four female pelvic floor conditions. Two clinician reviewers coded each video for misinformation on a dichotomised Likert item, giving a share of items judged to contain misinformation (18% of 74) — a CONTENT estimate with a stated denominator. The DISCERN quality result (96% scoring <3) is recorded as a QUALITY row per the QUALITY-vs-CONTENT rule.

estimates.measure_type: % of high-engagement female-pelvic-floor TikTok videos judged by clinician reviewers to contain misinformation
estimates.value_raw: Eighteen percent of the TikTok videos evaluated contained misinformation (n = 74 videos; by hashtag: #UTI 30%, #INC 20%, #OAB 0%, #POP 21%)
estimates.denominator: 74 TikTok videos: the top 20 by engagement in each of four female-pelvic-floor hashtags (#urinarytractinfection, #incontinence, #overactivebladder, #pelvicorganprolapse; only 14 POP videos met the >=100-engagement threshold), drawn from hashtag pools of 323, 972, 84 and 76 videos
estimates.definition: Mean of the two reviewers' 5-point Likert ratings of the statement that the video contained misinformation was > 3 (i.e. reviewers agreed or strongly agreed misinformation was present)
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; operationalised as reviewer agreement on a 'five-point Likert scale for misinformation' adapted from Tam et al., where 'A score > 3 indicated the TikTok video contained misinformation'
estimates.source_quote: Most TikTok videos (96%) had poor quality of information (DISCERN score <3), and 18% of TikTok videos contained misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 4; also Abstract; Table 1 row 'Misinformation > 3 (%)'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two reviewers specialising in female pelvic floor disorders, blinded to publisher biography and posting date, rated videos in random order on a 5-point misinformation Likert adapted from Tam et al. (2022); a third person adjudicated disagreements on content category. Inter-rater concordance 77% for misinformation scores (90% for DISCERN). No external fact-check or guideline benchmark is cited; the standard is the two clinicians' expert judgement.
estimates.moderator_quote: Between July and August 2021, we identified all TikTok videos on the U.S. app with the following hashtags: #pelvicorganprolapse (n = 76), #urinarytractinfection (n = 323), #overactivebladder (n = 84), and #incontinence (n = 972). ... The videos were ranked by engagement, defined as the summed number of likes, comments, and shares. The top twenty videos were selected for further review
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated sample: only the top-20-by-engagement videos per hashtag, so this is the prevalence among the MOST POPULAR FPF videos, not among all FPF videos (the hashtag pools contained 1,455 videos in total). The four hashtag-specific shares (#UTI 30/100, #INC 20%, #OAB 0%, #POP 21%) fall in the same country x platform x measure cell as this row and are nested inside it, so they were not split into separate rows; they are recorded here and in missed_or_uncertain. Quote replaced with the abstract sentence carrying the same value: in the Results section the same statement is split by 'Author Manuscript' watermark lines ('Eighteen percent of the TikTok videos evaluated' / 'contained misinformation. #OAB had the lowest percentage of videos that contained / misinformation (0%), followed by #INC (20%), #POP (21%), and #UTI (30%). The inter- / rater concordance was 90% for DISCERN scores and 77% for misinformation scores.'), so no contiguous span of it exists in the .txt rendering.

estimates.measure_type: % of high-engagement female-pelvic-floor TikTok videos with poor consumer-health-information quality (mean DISCERN score < 3)
estimates.denominator: The same 74 top-engagement TikTok videos across four female-pelvic-floor hashtags
estimates.definition: Overall mean DISCERN score below 3 (DISCERN is a 16-item validated instrument for the quality of consumer health information on treatment choices)
estimates.misinfo_def: Not a misinformation definition: DISCERN measures information quality (reliability, presentation of treatment choices, overall quality), not truth or falsity
estimates.source_quote: The majority of TikTok videos (96%) were of low quality in terms of medical information (overall mean DISCERN score < 3).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two FPF-specialist reviewers completed the 16-question DISCERN instrument for each video; inter-rater concordance 90%. The authors themselves note DISCERN was 'less suitable for the short video durations' and that 'there are not universally accepted DISCERN scoring guidelines'.
estimates.moderator_quote: Reviewers also completed the DISCERN tool, a 16-question validated instrument designed to judge the quality of consumer health information.
estimates.notes: QUALITY by the governing rule: DISCERN scores information quality, and a wholly accurate video can score < 3 (e.g. for lacking clear objectives or not covering treatment choices). Must be excluded from prevalence pooling; kept for the appendix only. The 96% figure is five times the paper's own misinformation prevalence (18%), a clear illustration of the quality-vs-falsity gap.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Hashtag-level misinformation prevalences (#UTI 30%, #INC 20%, #OAB 0%, #POP 21%; Table 1) and hashtag-level DISCERN<3 shares (100%, 95%, 100%, 86%) are stated but are nested subsamples of the same country x platform x measure cell; extracting them alongside the pooled figure would double-count, so they are logged in the value_raw and notes fields rather than as rows. (2) Mean misinformation Likert scores (#UTI 2.9, #INC 2.6, #OAB 2.0, #POP 2.2) and mean DISCERN scores (1.8, 1.7, 2.0, 2.0) are scale means with no share attached beyond the dichotomised shares already extracted, so no scale_score rows were made. (3) Correlations between misinformation score and shares/likes/engagement (r = 0.37, 0.23, 0.25 etc.) are associations, not prevalence. (4) Publisher-type percentages (healthcare worker 35-80%, layperson 20-30%, commercial 0-35%, physician 5-50%) describe who posts, not misinformation prevalence. (5) Engagement means (likes, comments, shares by hashtag) are counts, not shares. (6) Third-party figures quoted in the introduction ('one in five Americans consult TikTok before seeking medical attention'; pelvic floor disorders affect 'about a quarter of women') are cited from elsewhere and excluded by R8. (7) Judgement call for an adjudicator: the misinformation instrument is a single Likert item on which reviewers rate their AGREEMENT that misinformation is present, dichotomised at >3, with only 77% concordance — a weaker instrument than explicit fact-check adjudication; I coded it CONTENT (explicit misinformation coding by domain experts) rather than QUALITY, but it sits closer to the boundary than a fact-checked corpus would.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis, IRB-exempt. Frame: all videos on the U.S. TikTok app under four condition hashtags collected July-August 2021 (#pelvicorganprolapse n=76, #urinarytractinfection n=323, #overactivebladder n=84, #incontinence n=972); videos ranked by engagement (likes+comments+shares) and the top 20 per hashtag screened against inclusion criteria (>=100 engagements, English, adult human women, on-topic), yielding 74 videos (only 14 for POP). Two reviewers specialising in FPF disorders, blinded to publisher biography and posting date, viewed videos in random order and scored each on a 5-point misinformation Likert (adapted from Tam et al.; >3 = contains misinformation) and the 16-item DISCERN instrument; a third reviewer adjudicated content-category disagreements. Inter-rater concordance reported as 90% (DISCERN) and 77% (misinformation); no kappa. Analyses in SAS 9.4; no missing data. Main limitations: rank-truncated non-random sample of only the most-engaged videos, single-item misinformation scale, and DISCERN's poor fit to short-form video (acknowledged by the authors).
rob.item6_quote: Coders rated each video on a 5-point Likert scale adapted from Tam et. al for misinformation, i.e., 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neutral, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree that the video contained misinformation8. A score > 3 indicated the TikTok video contained misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Eighteen percent of the TikTok videos evaluated contained misinformation.
